doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

chapter: Creative ambitions and the jazz business
title: The $9,000 concert, Symphony for Six and the 'jazz' label
summary: Self-financed concert with mixed reviews; comparison with John Zorn who avoids the jazz label.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. Which is not to say — the way it works, that part of my career, it’s like this part of my career, I have a good time, I love these guys, I love playing the music and I make money and every year, I mean the jobs are fine. I mean here we are in this nice hotel. But for doing the other kind of stuff, it means using the money I make for that too, to like finance a concert, finance a record, finance this or that. And it gets increasingly hard for me to do, especially if I do that I mean just to give you one example, a couple of years ago I did a concert. I tried to get an NEA grant. I’d gotten a couple before but this one, they’re getting harder and harder to get. I didn’t get it, no funding at all. So I spent $9,000 of my own on a concert, and Mike Brecker was there, Chris Potter — I put together a great band, rehearsed all this new music. One of the things that I did, which I was interested in doing — the idea of the concert was kind of to use longer forms, kind of like classical forms, in a jazz context. So one of the things I wrote was this thing called “Symphony for Six,” which was in a symphony form, but for sextet. And it was all using this new harmonic stuff that I’m working on. And Chip Deffaa from The Post was there and he loved it. He wrote a really nice review. Peter Watrous was there from The Times and he didn’t, he just didn’t get it. And so he wrote, you know, just a very, very dismissive article. And so that’s not enough to stop me and say well hell I’m not going to do this. Of course I’m going to do it but it makes me think, is it worth it to spend $9,000 and all I end up with is a bad review in the Times? So it just makes me think that as far as — one of the things that I’ve kind of decided is that the label jazz is a very tricky thing these days. And I’ve noticed this with people like John Zorn, who’s been very successful, and I mean again like I don’t mean to — I like the group he’s got, Masada, with Dave Douglas. I love — I’ve heard some of his orchestral stuff. He’s a very talented guy. He’s also a very shrewd guy, and one of the things that’s shrewd about him is that he never © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

tried, or he tried to get himself over as this “downtown scene” musician, avoiding the label jazz, avoiding the comparisons with Coltrane and the young lions and the black and white thing and whatever — he just sidesteps that and he finds his audience and he gets his — he establishes his way. And I’m kind of finding the same thing. If I try to promote this as jazz you run up into a million hurdles from all kinds of directions. If I on the other hand go into a contemporary classical music direction I find that it’s like all these barriers break away.
